question:
Patient note:
A 38-year-old man employed as an overnight security guard was transported to the emergency department by ambulance at 05:10 after discovering that his third bowel movement of the night had rendered the toilet bowl “jet-black and sticky like roofing tar,” an observation he had never encountered before; the episode was accompanied by a pungent, metallic odor and required multiple flushes to clear. He recalled that earlier in the shift he felt a cramping epigastric ache relieved briefly by antacids from the vending machine, but over the subsequent four hours the discomfort became sharper, radiated slightly toward the back, and culminated in two loose, dark stools that progressively deepened in color. He denied vomiting, chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations beyond feeling his heart “pounding,” easy bruising, jaundice, or swelling of the ankles. There was no history of chronic liver problems, viral hepatitis, biliary disease, excessive alcohol consumption, or abnormal liver function tests on prior employment screenings. He is usually able to jog two miles three times per week without exertional limitation and sleeps flat without pillows. His only chronic medical condition is intermittent tension headaches for which he has ingested over-the-counter ibuprofen 600 mg three or four times daily during the past ten days while helping a friend move; he takes no prescription medications, avoids herbal products, and has never been exposed to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug warnings from a physician. He neither smokes nor uses illicit drugs and drinks beer socially no more than once monthly. Family history is notable for a father with type 2 diabetes and a mother with asthma; there are no relatives with peptic ulcer disease, bleeding disorders, cirrhosis, or heart-pump weakness. En route, paramedics reported that he appeared pale and diaphoretic but was awake, oriented, and able to recount events in detail. On arrival, before any intravenous line, crystalloid infusion, vasoactive medication, proton-pump inhibitor, antifibrinolytic, blood product, or antiemetic had been given, he lay supine on the gurney breathing rapidly yet speaking in full sentences. A manual blood pressure cuff on the right arm level with the mid-sternum registered 85/48 mm Hg, and a three-lead cardiac monitor displayed a narrow-complex tachycardia fluctuating between 148 and 152 beats per minute, which matched a thready radial pulse of 150 beats per minute by palpation. Respiratory rate was 26 per minute, oral temperature 36.7 °C, and oxygen saturation 97 % on ambient air. Capillary refill time exceeded four seconds; skin was cool and clammy, especially over the forearms; conjunctivae were markedly blanched, though sclerae remained anicteric. The pharynx showed no fresh or clotted blood. Jugular venous pulsation was not elevated at 45°, carotid upstrokes were brisk but weak, and peripheral pulses were barely palpable at the dorsalis pedis bilaterally. Cardiac auscultation revealed a rapid, regular S1 and S2 without murmur, gallop, or rub. Lungs were clear to auscultation throughout all fields. The abdomen was scaphoid, bowel sounds were hyperactive, and deep palpation elicited mild tenderness in the epigastrium without guarding, rebound, hepatosplenomegaly, or palpable masses; a succussion splash was absent, and there were no cutaneous stigmata of chronic liver disease such as spider angiomas, palmar erythema, or caput medusae. Extremities showed no edema or cyanosis. A focused neurologic screen demonstrated an alert individual answering appropriately to person, place, and time with equal, reactive pupils and 5/5 strength in all extremities, though he complained of light-headedness when attempting to sit upright. A single 16-gauge peripheral catheter was then inserted in the left antecubital fossa solely for diagnostic phlebotomy; at that snapshot he had received neither fluids nor medications. Point-of-care laboratory analysis performed twelve minutes later, still prior to any therapeutic intervention, revealed a hemoglobin of 7.8 g/dL, hematocrit 24 %, mean corpuscular volume 88 fL, platelet count 236 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 9.1 × 10⁹/L, blood urea nitrogen 83 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.0 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL on employment physical seven months ago), sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, glucose 98 mg/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.07. A 12-lead electrocardiogram printed simultaneously corroborated sinus tachycardia at 150 bpm with normal intervals and no ischemic changes. Upright portable chest radiography revealed clear lung fields and a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette; a single supine abdominal film displayed a nonspecific gas pattern without free air. Rectal examination performed immediately afterward produced a finger coated with thick, tarry feces that turned the guaiac card an intense blue within seconds, confirming the presence of upper gastrointestinal blood. The patient remained nil per os on continuous cardiac and pulse-oximetry monitoring while type-and-screen, urgent gastroenterology consultation, and resuscitation protocols were activated, all before the initiation of crystalloid resuscitation or transfusion.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score using pretreatment findings:
- BUN 83 mg/dL (≥70 mg/dL) → 6.
- Hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL (male, <10 g/dL) → 6.
- Systolic BP 85 mm Hg (<90) → 3.
- Pulse 150/min (≥100) → 1.
- Melena: black, tarry stool confirmed on examination → 1.
- Syncope: light-headedness without loss of consciousness → 0.
- Hepatic disease and heart failure: neither present → 0 each.
Sum: 6 + 6 + 3 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 17.
Final answer: 17
